case_name: Webster-Tweel v. Royal Trust Corporation of Canada
text:
Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation:
Webster-Tweel v. Royal Trust Corporation of Canada, 2010 ABQB 139

Date:

20100225

Docket:

0601 10061

Registry:

Calgary

Between:

Brenda Webster-Tweel

Applicant

-
and -

Royal Trust Corporation of Canada and
Hugh G. Hallward

Respondents

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of
the

Honourable Mr. Justice C.S. Brooker

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

This is an application for an accounting of various trusts whose proper
law is the laws of Quebec but whose assets are located in Alberta. The
Respondents are the trustees of these various trusts.

Procedural History

[
2
]

On August 24, 2006, the Applicant, Brenda Webster-Tweel, filed an
Originating Notice in this Court seeking an accounting of three different sets
of trusts.

[
3
]

On February 28, 2007, the Respondents filed a Motion to Institute
Proceedings for a Declaratory Judgment in the Quebec Superior Court seeking a
declaration that the proper law and the laws governing the administration of
the trusts are the laws of Quebec and that the laws of Quebec also govern the
Respondents' duty to account for the various trusts. In a decision, dated
November 1, 2007, the Quebec Superior Court dismissed the Respondents' application
for declaratory judgment noting "the Court concludes that there is a form
of
lis pendens
between the proceedings pending in Alberta and those
sought in Quebec. There is no longer any legal basis for the Motion for
declaratory judgment and such an action will not resolve in a complete and
final manner the litigation between the parties."

[
4
]

On March 26, 2007, the Respondent, Royal Trust Corporation of Canada
("Royal Trust"), filed a Notice of Motion seeking that the action be
struck for forum
non conveniens
on the basis that the Province of Quebec
was the more appropriate and convenient forum for the trial. On July 4, 2007,
the Respondent, Hugh G. Hallward, filed a Notice of Motion seeking the same
relief.

[
5
]

By an order dated July 30, 2007, Justice A. MacLeod dismissed the
Respondents' applications. MacLeod, J. declined to decide whether Alberta or
Quebec law was the proper law of the trusts and the law applicable to
accounting for the trusts. On October 5, 2007, the Respondents each filed a
Civil Notice of Appeal in the Court of Appeal of Alberta appealing Justice
MacLeod's Order. On January 18, 2008, the Court of Appeal dismissed the
Respondents' appeal. The Court concluded "[MacLeod, J.'s] conclusion that
Alberta is the most convenient forum in which to seek an accounting is not in
error."

[
6
]

With the jurisdiction issue resolved, the remaining issues to be decided
are whether the Respondents are required to account to Brenda Webster-Tweel for
the various trusts and whether the laws of Quebec or Alberta apply to this
determination.

Facts

[
7
]

Brenda Webster-Tweel is the daughter of Lorne Charles Webster. She is
the granddaughter of Colin Webster.

[
8
]

Brenda Webster-Tweel is requesting the accounting for three separate
sets of trusts: the Colin Webster Trusts, the Protective Trust and the
Webster-Tweel Trust, which is one of the Children's and Grandchildren's Trusts.
She seeks the accounting for the entire period from the time of each trust's
inception.

[
9
]

The Respondent, Royal Trust, is a trustee for all three sets of trusts.
The Respondent, Hallward, is a trustee for the Children's and Grandchildren's
Trusts only.

The Colin Webster Trusts

[
10
]

Colin Webster settled three
inter vivos
trusts in 1942, 1943 and
1944 (collectively the "Colin Webster Trusts"). The relevant
provisions in the Colin Webster Trusts may be summarized as follows:

(a)        In
each case, the trust property was given to Lorne Charles Webster and the
trustee had the discretion to encroach upon the capital of the trust property
for Lorne's benefit. At para. 3 of the 1942 Deeds of Donation and Trust:

The Trustee may also in their
sole discretion make over to the Donee or otherwise use for him from time to
time any portions of the capital of the Trust Property in addition to any
revenues; the whole in the sole discretion of the Trustees and
without obligation
on their part or on the part of the Donee to account further for any capital so
used by them
.

The 1943 and 1944 Deeds contain a
substantially similar provision, but specify the acceptable uses for the
capital to be "for his education, support, maintenance or general
welfare".

(b)        Upon
Lorne's death, the net revenue from the remaining capital in the Colin Webster
Trusts was to be paid to his wife (at para. 9 of the 1942 Deed and para. 8 of
the 1943 and 1944 Deeds). Upon his wife's death or re-marriage, the revenue was
to be shared by Lorne's children, equally. This equal distribution was again
subject to the same provisions allowing encroachment on the capital for the
benefit of the donees (at para. 4 of the Deeds).

(c)        The
Colin Webster Trusts contained a mechanism to resolve disagreements between the
trustees by referring these disputes to the solicitor for the Montreal Trust
Company, the Montreal Trust Company being an entity only in the Province of
Quebec. At para. IV(a) of the Deeds: "in any cases in which a majority of
the Trustees cannot agree, reference shall be made to the Solicitor for the
time being of Montreal Trust Company whose decision shall be final."

(d)        The
Colin Webster Trusts also included the following regarding trustee vacancies:
"The Trustees may at any time fill any vacancy by the appointment of any
reliable Trust Company having an office in the said City of Montreal" (at
para. IV(f) of the 1942 and 1943 Deeds) and "Any individual Trustee
hereunder resigning or for any other reason ceasing to be a Trustee after the
Donee has attained the full age of majority, shall not be replaced, and upon
the Donee dying, resigning or ceasing to be a Trustee the said THE ROYAL TRUST
COMPANY shall be and thereafter continue to be the sole Trustee hereunder"
(at para. IV(f) of the 1944 Deed).

[
11
]

Additional funds were added to the capital of the 1944 trust in 1945,
1946 and 1947 without changing the terms governing the trust.

[
12
]

The trustees for the Colin Webster Trusts were all from Quebec.

[
13
]

Colin Webster, Lorne Webster and Lorne's wife were all living in Quebec
at the time the trusts were created.

[
14
]

The Deeds to the Colin Webster Trust and subsequent amendments were
drafted by Quebec legal practitioners. These Deeds were registered in the
registry office for the registration division of Montreal.

[
15
]

In 1978, the administration of the Colin Webster Trusts was transferred
to the Royal Trust's Calgary office. The Royal Trust was the sole trustee. It
was suggested that this transfer was made to take advantage of favourable
capital gains legislation.

[
16
]

Before 1998, the main assets in the Colin Webster Trusts were shares in
Island City Investments Ltd. ("Island City"), an Alberta Corporation.
The Colin Webster Trusts also had shares in other properties. In December 1998,
the shares in Island City were transferred to a trust settled by Lorne Webster
on December 23, 1998 (the "Protective Trust", discussed below).

[
17
]

The Colin Webster Trusts currently have minimal assets. When asked what
assets remain in the Colin Webster Trusts, Garry Kaye, the Senior Trust Advisor
with Royal Trust, replied: "I believe they may have a dollar in them, or
something of that nature."

[
18
]

From 1978 until the Colin Webster Trusts stopped earning income, taxes
were paid by the Colin Webster Trusts as Alberta residents. The records and
accounts pertaining to the Colin Webster Trusts are maintained by the Royal
Trust's office in Calgary, Alberta.

The Protective Trust

[
19
]

On December 23, 1998, Lorne Webster created the Lorne Charles Webster
Protective Trust (the "Protective Trust"). The relevant portions of
the Protective Trust may be summarized as follows:

(a)        Lorne
Webster was the sole beneficiary under the Protective Trust and the income from
the Protective Trust was to be paid to him, according to how much of this
income he requested, during his lifetime (at para. 3(a) of the Deed).

(b)        Upon
the death of Lorne Webster, the trust property devolves in accordance with
provisions in a marriage contract or failing this, provisions of any valid will
or failing this, the law of intestacy of the jurisdiction in which Lorne
Webster was domiciled on his death (at para. 3(c)).

(c)        There
was a choice of law provision at para. 12:

The Parties agree that
the
proper law of the trusts herein established shall be the law of Quebec although
the law governing the administration of the trust may vary from time to time
.
Should for any reason ROYAL TRUST CORPORATION OF CANADA not be able to act or
continue to act as Trustee hereunder, it shall be replaced by THE ROYAL TRUST
COMPANY of Montreal.

[emphasis added]

(d)        The
Deed makes other explicit references to the laws of Quebec: when referencing
the beneficiaries obligations on separation, divorce or death (at para. 6) and
when stipulating that "the Trustees shall be entitled to reasonable
remuneration for their services as contemplated in the
Civil Code of
Quebec
" (at para. 10).

(e)        The
Deed also makes several implicit references to Quebec law, including a
reference to the
Civil Code of Québec (C.C.Q.)
, S.Q. 1991, c. 64 concept
of trust patrimony (at para. 2) and the Quebec document 'institution
contractuelle' (at para. 3(c)).

(f)         There
is also a provision that allows the trustee to make investments and establish
accounts with custodians of the assets anywhere in Canada or elsewhere (at
para. 8).

[
20
]

As noted above, the shares in Island City were transferred from the
Colin Webster Trusts to the Protective Trust. These shares formed the majority
of the assets in the Protective Trust.

[
21
]

The Deed was drafted by Quebec notaries and executed by Lorne Webster in
Quebec.

[
22
]

Lorne Webster was residing in Quebec at the time the Protective Trust
was settled.

[
23
]

The Deed named the Calgary office of the Royal Trust as trustee. The
Protective Trust was administered by Gary Kaye in Calgary. The Royal Trust
remained the sole trustee of the Protective Trust for the duration of its
existence.

[
24
]

At all times, taxes were paid by the Protective Trust as an Alberta
resident. The records pertaining to the Protective Trust are maintained by the
Royal Trust's office in Calgary, Alberta.

[
25
]

On the same day the Protective Trust was settled, the Marriage Contract
between Lorne Webster and his wife, Beverley Meredith Evans was amended to
address the devolution of the Protective Trust property (the "1998
Marriage Contract"), as anticipated by para. 3(c) of the Protective Trust
(summarized at para. 19(b), above).

[
26
]

The marriage contract provided that a gift of all shares in Island City
be made to the Trustee of the Protective Trust which was to be held in trust.
The net revenues from this new trust was to be paid to Beverley Evans, for her
lifetime (at para. 2 of the 1998 Marriage Contract). Other provisions existed
for the support, maintenance, and welfare of Lorne Webster's children and
grandchildren.

Children's and Grandchildren's Trust

[
27
]

On May 2, 2000, the 1998 Marriage Contract was amended to create a new
set of trusts upon Lorne Webster's death (the "2000 Marriage
Contract"). This 2000 Marriage Contract was entered into when both Lorne
Webster and Beverly Evans were residents of Quebec. The Marriage Contract was
created by a Quebec practitioner and executed by a Quebec notary.

[
28
]

On the same day, additional assets were added by Lorne Webster to the
Protective Trust through an Amendment to Protective Trust.

[
29
]

The relevant provisions of the 2000 Marriage Contract may be summarized
as follows:

(a)        Upon
the death of Lorne Webster, the property in the Protective Trust would be
gifted to the trustee to be held in trust and divided into a "Spousal
Trust" and a "Children's and Grandchildren's Trust" (at para.
2).

(b)        The
contract contains the following choice of law provision for the trusts at para.
20:

The Parties agree that the proper
law of the trusts herein established shall be the law of Quebec although the
law governing the administration of the trusts may vary from time to time as
determined in writing by the Trustees acting together. The Trustees confirm
that the Trust Property has been, and is presently, administered in Alberta.

(c)        There
are references to the Trustee's administration powers which are to be in
accordance with articles of the
Civil Code of Québec
: "the Husband
hereby confers upon the Trustees the powers of full administration of the
property of others in accordance with Articles 1306 and 1307 CCQ..." (at
para. 15).

(d)        There
are numerous references to the laws of Quebec, including: family patrimony of
spouses and the corresponding
Civil Code of Québec
provisions (at p. 2),
the purpose of the document purported to be in accordance with
article 1808
of
the
Civil Code of Québec
(at p. 2) and an election can be made as
permitted under the
Québec
Taxation Act
(at
para. 15
(l)).

[
30
]

The legal effect of the 2000 Marriage Contract was explained to Brenda
Webster-Tweel on May 25, 2000, in a meeting with legal counsel for the
Protective Trust and representatives from the Royal Trust.

[
31
]

In December 2004, Lorne Webster died and subsequent to his death, the
Spousal Trust and Children's and Grandchildren's Trust were formed pursuant to
the 2000 Marriage Contract. Brenda Webster-Tweel is a beneficiary of the
Children's and Grandchildren's Trusts. In particular, Brenda Webster-Tweel is
the beneficiary of the "Webster-Tweel Trust".

[
32
]

On July 19, 2005, Garry Kaye of Royal Trust wrote to Brenda
Webster-Tweel informing her that a capital distribution would be made from the
Protective Trust into the Webster-Tweel Trust. The letter also outlined that
the Children's and Grandchildren's Trusts would be receiving 43% of the capital
in the Protective Trust, and that $1,200,000 would be transferred to the
Webster-Tweel Trust at that time and a further $800,000 at a later time.

[
33
]

The 2000 Marriage Contract also appointed the Royal Trust and Hugh G.
Hallward, as trustees. The Royal Trust's Calgary office was noted as an
intervenant on the document. Hugh G. Hallward was noted as being from Quebec.
In practice, the day to day management of the trusts rests with the Royal Trust
in Calgary and not with Mr. Hallward in Quebec.

[
34
]

At all times taxes were paid by the Children's and Grandchildren's Trust
as Alberta residents. The records and accounts pertaining to the Children's and
Grandchildren's Trust are maintained by the Royal Trust's Calgary office.

Request for Accounting

[
35
]

Brenda Webster-Tweel asserts that she has been asking for an accounting
from the Trustees of the Colin Webster Trusts, the Protective Trust and the
Children's and Grandchildren's Trust for the last 25 years, or presumably from
the time the latter trusts came into existence.

[
36
]

On June 2, 2005, Brenda Webster-Tweel had a telephone conversation with
Garry Kaye of Royal Trust. The meeting took place by way of teleconference.
Presumably, during this meeting, Brenda Webster-Tweel was at her lawyer's
office in Toronto, Ontario, while Garry Kaye was in Calgary, Alberta. Brenda
Webster-Tweel asserts that during this conversation Gary Kaye agreed, on behalf
of Royal Trust, to provide an accounting to her. Garry Kaye's recollection of
this meeting is unclear as his counsel objected to questions addressing this
issue when Mr. Kaye was cross examined on his affidavit.

[
37
]

Following this conversation, an exchange of letters took place between
Garry Kaye and Brenda Webster-Tweel's counsel at the time. The following are
the relevant portions of this exchange:

(a)        On
October 21, 2005, Brenda's counsel wrote the following to Garry Kaye:

Brenda Tweel has been requesting
an accounting from the trustees over the past 10 years.
Following our
meeting, I thought that the accounting would be forthcoming. It appears that it
has not been
.

My instructions are to apply to
Court to compel an accounting, if one is not promptly produced. That will only
result in increased costs. I trust this will not be necessary.

Please advise when I can expect
to receive the full accounting.

[emphasis added]

(b)        Garry
Kaye's response on October 26, 2005 indicated that Royal Trust was willing, at
that time, to provide 15 years of records for the trusts:

Firstly, with respect to an
accounting from the trustees, we have been able to determine that it is
possible to produce copies of trust statements dating back approximately
fifteen years.
We will start copying those statements now, and we will be
shipping them directly to your office, if that is satisfactory
. We expect
that the volume of statements could be quite significant. We will provide you
these statements in a spirit of transparency. As you may also know, these
statements and other statements had already been given to Mr. Lorne Webster,
who during his lifetime was, under Quebec law, the sole actual beneficiary of
the trusts.

[emphasis added]

(c)        On
January 10, 2006, Brenda's counsel wrote the following to Garry Kaye:

In your letter dated October 26,
2005, you advised that you were in the process of copying some of the records
that we had requested. I understood from your letter that a copy of these
records would be sent to me shortly after the date of your letter. I note that
nothing has been received to date.

My request for records goes back
to June 3, 2005. As noted in my letter dated October 21, 2005, my client has
been asking for the accounting over the last ten years.

Please forward the accounting at
this time.

(d)        On
February 9, 2006, Brenda's counsel again wrote to Garry Kaye asking for the
accounting documents and advising that: "if you do not provide the
requested documentation, my instructions are to proceed with an application to
court."

(e)        On
February 9, 2006, Royal Trust replied through a letter written by its counsel.
Royal Trust advised that its position was that Quebec law applied to all of the
trusts and as such, Brenda Webster-Tweel was not entitled to an accounting for
the Colin Webster Trusts. Alternatively, Royal Trust advised that Brenda Webster-Tweel
could only receive an accounting for the three-year period prior to her request
based on limitations under the
Civil Code of Québec
. With respect to the
Protective Trust, Royal Trust's position was that no accounting was due to her
as she was not a beneficiary under these trusts. With respect to the
Webster-Tweel Trust, Royal Trust advised that she was entitled to receive
annual accounts.

(f)         Brenda's
counsel sent a reply on February 20, 2006 advising that litigation would be
commenced to settle the matter. In particular, he noted: "The trustee
agreed to provide the accounting in a discussion I had with Mr. Kaye on June 2,
2005."

[
38
]

For the Webster-Tweel Trust, Brenda has received detailed financial
statements for this trust since its inception in the form of 'Investment
Statements' and 'Capital and Revenue Transaction Statements'. She asserts,
however, that these documents leave 'unanswered questions' and are
insufficient. She has not specified what additional documents or information
she is seeking to obtain from the trustees.

[
39
]

There is no information as to the purpose for which Brenda Webster-Tweel
is requesting these accountings. The Respondent Hallward suggested three
possible reasons for Brenda Webster-Tweel's request: her right of enforcement,
her interest in determining the initial contents of the Webster-Tweel Trust,
and her general rights as a beneficiary.

Position of the Parties

Applicant's Position

[
40
]

The Applicant's position is that she is entitled to an accounting of
these trusts for the entire time each has been in existence based on the common
law obligations of the trustees.

[
41
]

For the Colin Webster Trusts, she argues that the law of administration
is that of Alberta because the administration was transferred from Quebec to
Alberta in 1978, the trustee's office since the transfer has been in Alberta,
the main assets of the trust are shares in an Alberta corporation, the income
tax returns for this trust are filed as a resident of Alberta, and taxes were
paid as a resident of Alberta.

[
42
]

For the Protective Trust, she argues that the law of administration is
that of Alberta because the choice of law clause within the Protective Trust
specifies that the law of administration may vary from time to time. The
Applicant asserts that this clause should be interpreted to mean the law of
administration is wherever the actual administration of the trusts takes place,
in this case, being Alberta.

[
43
]

For the Children's and Grandchildren's Trusts, the Applicant argues that
the choice of law clause contained in the 2000 Marriage Contract that is said
to apply to these trusts must be interpreted to be an express choice of law
denoting the present law of administration to be in Alberta.

[
44
]

The Applicant further argues that pursuant to the laws of Alberta, this
Court should exercise its discretion to order Royal Trust to provide an
accounting based on the common law duty owed by trustees to account to all
individuals with interests in the trusts. The Applicant asserts that the
following factors warrant the Courts exercise of its discretion in the
Applicant's favour: the promise Royal Trust made to provide an accounting
through the telephone meeting on June 2, 2005 and subsequent correspondence,
the records are in possession of Royal Trust in its Calgary offices, the
amounts within the trusts are significant "into the tens of millions of
dollars", and suspicion has arisen from the trustees' refusal to provide
an accounting.

[
45
]

Alternatively, the Applicant argues that it is entitled to the
accounting for the last 15 years for all three trusts based on an agreement by
Royal Trust to provide the accounting. The Applicant asserts this agreement
arose from the telephone meeting on June 2, 2005 and subsequent correspondence.

Respondent's Position

[
46
]

The Respondent Royal Trust's position is that Brenda Webster-Tweel is
not entitled to an accounting for any of the trusts.

[
47
]

For the Webster-Tweel Trust, Royal Trust argues that any obligation to
account has already been met as Royal Trust provided detailed statements
pertaining to this trust and the Protective Trust from December 16, 2004.

[
48
]

For the Colin Webster Trusts and the Protective Trust, Royal Trust
argues that since the proper law of the trusts is Quebec then the laws of
Quebec should also govern whether Brenda Webster-Tweel is entitled to an
accounting. Royal Trust argues this based on the presumption of unity, which
requires one law to apply to all issues relating to a trust, or, alternatively,
because the laws of Quebec apply to the issue of whether the Applicant is
entitled to an accounting for these trusts.

[
49
]

On the alternative argument, Royal Trust further argues that the initial
law applicable to the administration of both the Colin Webster Trusts and the Protective
Trust was Quebec and was never changed to Alberta. Royal Trust argues that it
is the laws of Quebec that govern whether changes in the laws applicable to
administration are valid and since there was no court order, which is required
by Quebec law to change the laws applicable to administration, the laws
applicable to administration did not change. Royal Trust also argues that
changing the location of assets or the trustees is insufficient to change the
laws applicable to administration.

[
50
]

To support the argument that Quebec laws should apply, Royal Trust notes
the many references to the laws of Quebec within the deeds for the trusts and
the 2000 Marriage Contract, in particular a reference to the
Civil Code of
Québec
which discusses administration of trusts. Royal Trust also argues
that the object of the Colin Webster Trusts and the Protective Trust were both
to provide for Lorne Webster, who resided in Quebec.

[
51
]

Royal Trust then relies on its expert, Dr. Jeffrey Talpis to prove that
when Quebec law is applied, only Lorne Webster is entitled to an accounting.

[
52
]

Alternatively, Royal Trust argues that even if the law of Alberta were
to apply to the accounting issue, the Applicant is still not entitled to an
accounting. For the Colin Webster Trusts, Royal Trust argues that this Court
should exercise its discretion to refuse an accounting as it is not reasonable
to order records going back more than 60 years to be produced, an account was
provided to the immediate beneficiary of the trusts, the trusts are completed
and the trusts' objects are fulfilled. For the Protective Trust, Royal Trust
argues that Brenda Webster-Tweel was not entitled to an accounting before 2004
as she was not a beneficiary and does not have standing for an accounting.

[
53
]

In addition to the arguments presented by Royal Trust, the Respondent
Hallward further argues that the law of Quebec should apply to the Colin
Webster Trusts and Protective Trust because firstly, the trust deeds did not
specify that the laws of Alberta would govern the administration of the trusts
and secondly, the trustees and settlor did not draft any resolutions or make
any judicial applications to change the law of administration to Alberta.
Hallward's position is that any connections to Alberta are insufficient to
overturn the presumption of a unified trust law, and that, in this case, the
presumption is that all trust matters will be governed by the laws of Quebec.
Hallward relies in part on Dr. Talpis' expert opinion and in part on
jurisprudence from the Quebec courts to establish that if Quebec law were to be
applied, then any claim for accounting more than three years before the
Originating Notice was filed, on August 24, 2006, is statute-barred under
Quebec law.

[
54
]

The Respondent Hallward argues that, in any event, even if the laws of
Alberta were to apply to the accounting issue, this Court should exercise its
discretion to refuse an accounting as an accounting was already provided to
Lorne Webster and there is little Brenda Webster-Tweel can gain from such an
accounting. The Respondent Hallward also argues that any actions arising out of
the documents pertaining to transactions more than ten years before Brenda
Webster-Tweel filed her statement of claim in 1996 would be statute barred,
making it unreasonable to order an accounting for any records prior to 1996.
Hallward further argues that it is not reasonable to require Royal Trust to
account for over 60 years of records when Brenda Webster-Tweel's interest in
the Colin Webster Trusts and Protective Trust are tenous. In this regard,
Hallward's position is that Brenda has no interest in the Protective Trust and
her interest in the Colin Webster Trust is merely the right to a portion of the
interest in the one dollar remaining in the trust for her lifetime.

Issues

[
55
]

The issues to be determined are as follows:

1.         whether
the laws of Quebec or the laws of Alberta apply to determine whether the
Applicant is entitled to an accounting of the three trusts;

2.         whether,
based on the applicable law, the Applicant is entitled to an accounting of the
three trusts; and

3.         whether
this Court should issue an order requiring Royal Trust to provide accounting
records for the last 15 years on the basis of a contractual agreement between
Royal Trust and Brenda Webster-Tweel.

Discussion

1.         whether
the laws of Quebec or the laws of Alberta apply to determine whether the
Applicant is entitled to an accounting of the three trusts

[
56
]

There are several choice of law rules that are potentially engaged by
this analysis: the laws applicable to the validity of the trust, the laws
applicable to the administration of the trust, the laws applicable to
determining the scope of the rights of beneficiaries, the laws applicable to
enforcement of the rights of beneficiaries, and the laws applicable to a
variation of the laws applicable to the trust.

[
57
]

The applicable choice of law rules are those of the forum in which the
hearing is held. (
Castel and Walker: Canadian Conflict of Laws
, 6
th

ed., vol. 1, looseleaf (Ontario: LexisNexis, 2005) at p. 1-2). Since this
hearing is being heard in Alberta, it is the Alberta choice of law rules that
are applicable.

Choice of Law - Request for Accounting

[
58
]

At the outset, it is necessary to determine whether the matters at issue
pertain to validity or administration of trusts, or scope or enforcement of
rights. (See for example
Castel and Walker
, vol. 2 at p. 28-1)

Does the accounting form part of the validity or
administration of trusts?

[
59
]

At common law, a distinction is made between the validity and the
administration of a trust. This distinction was summarized by Prof. Waters in
Waters'
Law of Trusts in Canada
, 3d ed. (Toronto: ThomsonCarswell, 2005) at pp.
1379 and 1380:

Validity is an all-embracing term
including all those matters which are concerned with the initial validity of
the trust. In the conflict of laws, it is usual to distinguish formal validity
from essential validity... So in a trust, formal validity refers to the
validity of the mode in which the trust has been constituted; essential
validity will include the capacity of the settlor or testator to create the
trust, and the permissibility of the substantive provisions of the trust...

Administration is a term which
embraces all those issues that are exclusively concerned with the management or
administration of trust affairs. Administration covers such issues as who may
appoint, and be appointed as, a new trustee,
the powers and duties of
trustees
, trustee investments, the distinction between income and capital,
the liability of trustees for breach of trust and their rights of indemnity and
contribution. It will also include the administrative powers of the court, the
power to give advice, and to confer powers or authority upon trustees.

[emphasis added]

[
60
]

The distinction between the validity and administration of a trust was
further discussed by
Castel and Walker
, vol. 2 at p. 28-1:

Validity generally includes such
issues as the formal validity of the trust, the capacity of the settlor or
testator to create the trust, whether it can be revoked, and whether its
purpose is lawful. Administration is concerned with the management or
administration of trust affairs.

[
61
]

The definitions for 'validity' and 'administration' in
The Oxford
English Dictionary
, 2d ed.,
s.v.
"validity",
"administration" are as follows:

validity. 1. The quality of being
valid in law; legal authority, force, or strength.

administration. ... 6.
Law
.
The management and disposal of the estate of a deceased person by an executor
or administrator... 7. The action of administering something to others: a.
Dispensation (of a sacrament, of justice, etc.). b. Giving or application (of
remedies). c. Tendering (of an oath).

[
62
]

In
Schmidt v. Rosewood Trust Limited
,
[2003] UKPC 26, [2003] 3
All E.R. 76
the Privy Council considered that seeking the disclosure of trust
documents was an aspect of administration, at para. 66:

Their Lordships have already
indicated their view that a beneficiary's right to seek disclosure of trust
documents, although sometimes not inappropriately described as a proprietary
right, is best approached as one aspect of the court's inherent jurisdiction to
supervise (and where appropriate to intervene in) the administration of trusts.

[
63
]

It seems to me that the request for an accounting by Brenda
Webster-Tweel is an aspect of managing the trust. Any duty of the trustee to
account to beneficiaries arises out of its role in managing the trusts and the
accounts are created in the course of this management. Further, the request of
accounts are akin to the disclosure of documents sought in
Schmidt
,
which were considered to be an aspect of administration. Whether or not Brenda
is entitled to an accounting has no effect on the validity of the trusts themselves.
As such, I find that the request for accounting is more closely related to the
'administration' of the trusts than the 'validity' of the trusts.

Does the accounting form part of the scope or enforcement
of the rights of beneficiaries?

[
64
]

The English approach distinguishes between determining the scope of the
beneficiaries' rights and enforcement of these rights. This was summarized by
Dicey, Morris & Collins in
The Conflict of Laws
, 14th ed., vol. 2
(London: Sweet&Maxwell, 2006) at para. 29-058:

Enforcement of the rights of
beneficiaries. The law applicable to the trust will determine the nature and
extent of the beneficiaries' rights, but their enforcement is essentially a
procedural matter governed by the law of the court which has assumed
jurisdiction to administer the trust in question.

[
65
]

This English approach was considered by K. Thomas Grozinger in
"Conflict of Laws and Trusts of Movables in Canada: Determining the
Applicable Law for Essential Validity and Administration" (2004) 23
E.T.P.J. 301 at 370: "The enforcement of the rights of beneficiaries as
against the trustee appears to be a procedural matter governed by the law of
the court which has assumed jurisdiction to administer the trust in
question." Although this comment may be limited to situations where
beneficiaries are seeking to remove and replace trustees who are subject to the
personal jurisdiction of the court.

[
66
]

I find that whether or not Brenda Webster-Tweel is entitled to an
accounting of the various trusts goes to the nature and extent of her rights as
a beneficiary and is more than a procedural matter of enforcing an undisputed
right. Thus, the question of whether Brenda is entitled to an accounting is
governed by the laws applicable to the administration of the trust, as
discussed above.

Applicable Choice of Law Rule

The laws governing administration can be different than
the laws governing validity

[
67
]

The parties are in agreement that the laws of Quebec is the proper law
for all the trusts. The Repondents argued that there is a presumption that all
aspects of a trust should be governed by the proper law under a principle of
'unity'. The Applicant relied on the principle of 'dépeçage' that allows
different aspects of the trust to be governed by different laws.

[
68
]

In England and Australia, there is a principle of unity which dictates
that the validity and administration of trusts are governed by the same law.
See for example the English case of
Chellaram v. Chellaram
,
[1985] 1 All
E.R. 1043 (Ch.)
and the Australian case of
Re Webb Estate
(1992), 57
S.A.S.R. 193 (S.C.).

[
69
]

It is not clear, however, whether this principle of unity applies in
Canada. It appears that under the current state of the law in Canada, it is
possible for the law governing the administration of trusts to be different
from the law governing the validity of the trust. The current state of the law
was summarized by
Castel and Walker
, vol. 2

at p. 28-4:

Generally, the validity of a
trust, its construction and its effect are governed by the same law but
the
administration of the trust may be governed by a different law
. In England,
no distinction is made at common law between the validity, interpretation,
effect and administration of a trust because it is thought desirable that a
trust should be treated as a unit. However, in the absence of an express
choice,
some Canadian decisions favour the application to questions of
administration of the domestic law of the place of administration, which is
generally the place where the trustees or a majority of them reside or carry on
the business of the administration on the ground that the administration is
most significantly related to that place
.

[emphasis added]

[
70
]

A similar conclusion was reached by Prof. Waters in
Waters' Law of
Trusts in Canada
at p. 1379: "Since 1945, Canadian courts have drawn a
distinction between the validity of a trust and the administration of a
trust." For this proposition, he cites
Re Nanton
,
1948 CanLII 489 (MB KB)
, [1948] 2 W.W.R.
113 (Man. K.B.) and
Jewish National Fund v. Royal Trust Co.
,
1965 CanLII 49 (SCC)
, [1965]
S.C.R. 784.

[
71
]

This distinction between validity and administration was also confirmed
by Grozinger in his article at p. 376:

Common law experience suggests
that the law governing a trust of movables or an aspect of such a trust, such
as administration, will depend on the intention of the settlor/testator,
whether that intention is express or implied.

The Canadian common law
experience suggests that,
absent evidence of intention, different aspects of
a trust of movables - in particular administration and validity - may be
governed by different laws
.

[emphasis added]

[
72
]

Although not directly applicable to conflict of law issues between
provinces, the
International Conventions Implementation Act
, R.S.A.
2000, c. I-6, Sch. 1, art. 9 supports the principle that matters relating to
administration can be governed by different laws than those governing validity:

In applying this Chapter, a
severable aspect of the trust, particularly matters of administration, may be
governed by a different law.

[
73
]

The Protective Trust and the 2000 Marriage Contract which establishes
the Webster-Tweel Trust also provide that the law governing administration can
be something other than the laws of Quebec: "the proper law of the trusts
herein established shall be the law of Quebec although the law governing the
administration of the trust may vary from time to time" (at para. 12 and
20, respectively).

[
74
]

Thus the issue is whether, in this situation, the law governing
administration is something other than the proper law of the trust.

Choice of Law Rule - Administration

[
75
]

The choice of law rule applicable to the administration of trusts was
summarized by
Castel and Walker
, vol. 2 at pp. 28-4 to 28-5:

With respect to matters of
administration that can be controlled by the terms of the trust,
the settlor
or testator should be able to designate a place whose internal law is to govern
the administration of the trust
whether or not that place is connected with
the trust... In the case of a trust created
inter vivos
,
if there is
no such designation by the settlor, the courts should apply the internal law of
the place to which the administration of the trust is most significantly
related or to which it is most closely connected
.

[emphasis added]

Where there is a corporate
trustee, and the settlor or testator carried out the arrangements for setting
up of the corporate trusteeship at a branch office, there should be a
presumption that he or she intended the law of the place where the branch office
is located to be the law of the administration.

[
76
]

Thus, the question to ask is what the settlor intended, and absent
evidence of intention, the inquiry turns to where the administration of the
trust is most closely connected.

[
77
]

The text of the trust deed may also reveal an
implied
choice of
law by the settlor as to the laws applicable to the administration of the
trusts. For example, a reference to the laws of a particular province applying
to an aspect of administration may show an intention that the laws of that
province should govern matters of trust administration in general (see
Grozinger's
article
at p. 326).

[
78
]

In
Waters' Law of Trusts in Canada
at p. 1392, Prof. Waters
confirms that for administration of trusts, "in the absence of an
effective choice, the court will apply the system of law with which the trust
has its most substantial connection." The Professor further discusses the
factors to consider in determining the most substantial connection. He writes,
"the residence or place of business of the trustees will be very
significant in this regard, since it is the trustees who carry out the
administration" and "other factors which will be relevant are the
location of the assets and of the beneficiaries."

[
79
]

In
Grozinger's article
, he even suggests that the residence of
the trustees is the determinative factor when selecting the appropriate law
respecting issues of administration. At p. 376:

As regards the choice of law
governing issues respecting the administration of a trust, the Canadian common
law suggests that
absent evidence of intention the relevant law is found by
determining the law of the place of administration of the trust. For trusts of
moveables, this is the place where the trustees exercising the power of the
administration reside
.

[emphasis added]

[
80
]

However, in his subsequent publication, "Conflict of Laws and
Trusts of Movables in Canada: An Update" (2005) 24 E.T.P.J. 285 at 286 to
287, Grozinger suggests that the residence of the trustees may simply create a
rebuttable presumption that the laws of that place govern the administration of
the trust.

[
81
]

When determining, more generally, the law with which a trust is most
closely connected, the
International Conventions Implementation Act
,
Sch. 1, art. 7 sets out the following factors:

In ascertaining the law with
which a trust is most closely connected reference shall be made in particular
to –

(a) the place of administration
of the trust designated by the settlor;

(b) the situs of the assets of
the trust;

(c) the place of residence or
business of the trustee;

(d) the objects of the trust and
places where they are to be fulfilled.

[
82
]

When discussing these factors,
Dicey, Morris & Collins
added
the following comments at para. 29-019:

... where the place of
administration is designated by the settlor, this will be a very strong
indicator of an implied choice of law...

The
situs
of the assets of
the trust may deserve little weight: the movables included in a trust are
usually intangible, e.g. stocks, shares and bonds; and the
situs
of an
intangible movable is to some extent a fiction...

The place of residence or
business of the trustee is a factor whose importance in the common law cases
varied from almost irrelevance to near decisiveness. Where the original
trustees are domiciled or habitually resident in different States, this factor
is likely to be of very little relevance; by contrast, if the trustees are
domiciled or habitually resident in the same State, or the settlor sets up a trust
company in a certain State, the factor may well be of considerable importance.

The final factor mentioned in
Art. 7 is the objects of the trust and their place of fulfilment. It is
suggested that little importance should be attached to this, since Art.7 is
concerned with the law of closest connection. Only if the objects of the
[trust] indicate to the court an objective factor relating the trust, such as
where the assets should be invested, or the trust administered, should this be
important.

[citations omitted]

[
83
]

Dicey, Morris & Collins
also note other factors that are
considered when determining where the closest connection is: "these will
include the domicile of the settlor ... the legal style of the trust
instrument, the domicile of the beneficiaries, and the place of execution of
the trust deed" (at para. 29-020).

[
84
]

It is also clear that the weight to be given to the various factors
varies with the circumstances (see
Dicey, Morris & Collins
at para.
29-020).

Choice of Law - Variation of Trusts

[
85
]

The common law recognizes that a settlor can provide within the trust
deeds the power to change the law governing the administration of a trust of
movables (see
Waters' Law of Trusts
at p. 1393,
Grozinger's article

at p. 377).

[
86
]

Absent express permission in the deed documents, it is not clear whether
courts in Canada are bound by the laws governing the trust when approving
variations to the law governing administration. The law is not clear as to
whether the variation is part of the administration of the trust or part of the
inherent jurisdiction of the forum court (see
Waters' Law of Trusts
at
p. 1393). In the international context,
Castel and Walker
suggest that
the approach of the English courts should be adopted in Canada: "the
courts when exercising jurisdiction to vary a trust must apply to the variation
the substantive law of the state governing the trust" (at vol. 2, p.
28-15).

[
87
]

A similar approach is suggested in
Waters' Law of Trusts
at p.
1394: "There is much to be said for a choice of law rule which makes it
clear that variation of a trust is governed by the proper law of the trust's
administration. This is the rule under the Convention, and it is consistent
with the results of both
Re Paget's Settlement
[
[1965] 1 All E.R. 58
(Eng. Ch. Div.)
]

and
Laing
[
[1981] A.J. No. 536 (Alta. Q.B.)
]
.
"

[
88
]

Thus, I am of the opinion that the laws applicable to the administration
of the trust also apply when determining if these laws have validly been changed.

Analysis

Colin Webster Trust

[
89
]

The Colin Webster Trust contains no choice of law clause. It does,
however, contain numerous references to entities in Quebec, including the
Montreal Trust Company to resolve disputes and trustee vacancies to be replaced
with trust companies with offices in Montreal. Additionally, at the time the
Colin Webster Trust was settled, all the trustees were from Quebec, Colin
Webster, Lorne Webster and Lorne's wife at the time were all living in Quebec,
and the documents were drafted and registered in Quebec.

[
90
]

Thus, I find that viewed in terms of an implied intention or the place
where the administration of the trust has the closest connection, the laws
applicable to administrative issues, at the time the Colin Webster Trust was
settled, were the laws of Quebec.

[
91
]

The question then becomes, whether the laws of administration changed
from Quebec to Alberta in 1978 when the trustee and assets of the trusts were
moved to Alberta.

[
92
]

The Respondents' expert, Dr. Talpis, provided written evidence that
"since January 1, 1994, it was possible for the trustees to request the
Court to change the law applicable to the administration from that of Quebec to
Alberta (articles 1294, 3111, para. 3 and 3108 CCQ)" (at para. 66). He then
referred to
article 1294
of the
Civil Code of Québec
as a
"requirement of court approval" to effectively change the law
governing administration (at para. 70).

[
93
]

I am satisfied that, in accordance with Dr. Talpis' opinion, a Quebec
court in 2008 would not consider that the law governing the administration of
the Colin Webster Trust changed to Alberta in absence of court approval for
such a change.

[
94
]

Thus, I conclude that the laws applicable to administrative issues for
the Colin Webster Trust are the laws of Quebec.

Protective Trust

[
95
]

The Protective Trust contains no express provision as to which laws
govern the administration of the trusts. Instead, the Protective Trust's choice
of law provision provides that the proper law of the trusts shall be Quebec and
"the law governing the administration of the trust may vary from time to
time". The Protective Trust also contains references to the laws of
Quebec. Most noteably, there is a provision which states that if the Royal
Trust ceases to act as trustee then it shall be replaced by the Royal Trust
Company of Montreal and that the trustees shall be paid remuneration in
accordance with the
Civil Code of Québec
. There is also a provision
which allows the trustee to make investments and establish investment accounts
anywhere in Canada or elsewhere.

[
96
]

With respect to the actual administration, since the Protective Trust
was created, Royal Trust was the sole trustee of the Protective Trust and
administered this trust in Alberta. Additionally, the majority of the assets
within the Protective Trust were held in Alberta and were investments in
Alberta corporations. Taxes for this trust were paid as an Alberta resident.

[
97
]

The Applicant argues that the Protective Trust choice of law provision
should be read to mean the law governing the administration of the trust is
wherever the trustee is located and changes whenever the trustee moves to a
different province. Since the trustee and majority of assets are in Alberta,
the Applicant's position is that Alberta law should govern matters of
administration. The Applicant further supports her argument by referencing the
choice of law provision in the 2000 Marriage Contract which specifies that
those trusts are being administered in Alberta. This seems to be a logical
conclusion when reading the choice of law provision in the Protective Trust on
its own. Additionally, as suggested by
Castel and Walker
, supra, since
the Royal Trust is a corporate trustee, there may be a presumption that, by
appointing an Alberta branch as trustee, Lorne Webster intended the laws of
Alberta to be the laws governing administration.

[
98
]

However, other provisions in the trust deed lead to the conclusion that
Lorne Webster intended the laws of Quebec to apply, at the outset, to matters
of administration. For example, the trustee is to be paid in accordance with
the
Civil Code of Québec
and the trustee is to be replaced with the
Royal Trust Company of Montreal, in Quebec. Since these provisions were
included with the knowledge that the trustee and majority of the assets would
be in Alberta, Lorne Webster indicated that, despite the connections with
Alberta, Quebec law continued to apply. With this in mind, it is also logical
to infer from the provision which allows investments to be made anywhere in
Canada and elsewhere that making such investments in another place will not
necessarily make the laws of that place applicable to matters of administration
for the entire trust.

[
99
]

Thus, I find that although the trustee and assets were in Alberta at the
time the Protective Trust was established, the interpretation that most closely
accords with the settlor's intention is that the laws of Quebec apply to
matters of administration while leaving open the possibility of changing this
law. As such, it is not necessary to decide whether the matters of
administration are most closely connected with Quebec or Alberta. Additionally,
from the evidence, there is nothing which would trigger a change to the law
governing the administration to any place other than Quebec.

[
100
]

Thus,
I conclude that the laws applicable to administrative issues for the Protective
Trust are the laws of Quebec.

Webster-Tweel Trust

[
101
]

The
Webster-Tweel Trust was created pursuant to terms of the 2000 Marriage
Contract. The 2000 Marriage Contract contained a provision which set out that
the proper law of the trusts was to be the laws of Quebec. It contained the
following pertaining to the laws governing administration at para. 20:

The law governing the
administration of the trusts may vary from time to time as determined in
writing by the Trustees acting together. The Trustees confirm that the Trust
Property has been, and is presently, administered in Alberta.

[
102
]

The
2000 Marriage Contract also contains a provision where Lorne Webster, the
settlor, confers upon the Trustees "the powers of full administration of
the property of others in accordance with Articles 1306 and 1307 CCQ" (at
para. 15).

[
103
]

As
such, it is not clear whether the trust was meant to be governed by Alberta or
Quebec law. In light of this ambiguity, the inquiry then turns to which
province is most closely connected with the Webster-Tweel Trust.

[
104
]

The
factors which support the application of Alberta law include the provision in
the 2000 Marriage Contract which confirms the Trust is administered in Alberta.
Also, the Royal Trusts' Calgary office was appointed as trustee and conducts
the day to day management of the Trust, and taxes for the Trust were paid as an
Alberta resident.

[
105
]

The
factors which support the application of Quebec law include that one of the
trustees appointed is a resident of Quebec and the 2000 Marriage Contract
specifically says that powers of administration of the property are granted in
accordance with articles of the
Civil Code of Québec
. Also, at the time
the 2000 Marriage Contract was signed, both Lorne Webster and his wife,
Beverley Evans, were residents of Quebec.

[
106
]

Neither
Alberta nor Quebec are clearly more closely connected to the administration of
the Webster-Tweel Trust. Both Alberta and Quebec are referenced in the 2000
Marriage Contract in the context of the administration of the Webster-Tweel
Trust.

[
107
]

In
light of my decision below, however, it is not necessary to determine whether
this trust was governed by Quebec or Alberta law.

2.         whether,
based on the applicable law, the Applicant is entitled to an accounting of the
three trusts

Colin Webster Trust and Protective Trust

Application of the laws of Quebec

[
108
]

As
discussed above, the applicable laws for the Colin Webster Trust and the
Protective Trust are the laws of Quebec.

[
109
]

Foreign
law must be proven as a fact and must be proven to the satisfaction of the
court by the party relying on the foreign law (
Castel and Walker
, vol. 1
at p. 7-1). In general, foreign law is proven by the testimony of an expert.
The competence and qualifications of the witness can be considered by a court
when deciding whether or not to accept the expert's opinion. However, if the
evidence of the expert witness is uncontradicted, a court will normally accept
it (
Castel and Walker
, vol. 1

at p. 7-5).

[
110
]

In
this case, the Respondents' called Dr. Jeffrey Talpis to prove the relevant
Quebec law. Dr. Talpis is well qualified to provide an opinion as to how the
laws of Quebec would apply to this situation. He is a full Professor at the law
school of the University of Montreal and is recognized as a leading authority
in private international law and in international and domestic estate, trust
and personal planning matters. He has been cited by the courts in Quebec and
elsewhere in Canada in more than 120 cases since 1995.

[
111
]

With
respect to the Colin Webster Trusts, Dr. Talpis opined as follows:

I am of the opinion that although
the Applicant is a future beneficiary under the [Colin Webster] Trusts she was
not entitled to annual accounts because the actual beneficiary, Lorne Webster,
was receiving them until his death in 2004 and thereafter, his widow is
entitled to the accounts as income beneficiary in his place.

[
112
]

With
respect to the Protective Trust, Dr. Talpis opined:

I am also of the opinion that
although the Applicant may be considered to be an interested person under the
Protective Trust, she was not entitled to annual accounts because the actual
beneficiary, Lorne Webster, received them until his death in 2004, at which
date the Protective Trust terminated.

[
113
]

These
opinions were developed after a thorough review of the
Civil Code of Québec

and the interaction between different provisions. In light of this, and his
qualifications as an expert, I accept Dr. Talpis' conclusions that the
Applicant is not entitled to an account under Quebec law.

[
114
]

In
light of this finding, it is unnecessary to address counsel's argument with
respect to the applicable limitations periods for the request for accountings.

Application of the laws of Alberta

[
115
]

I
have also concluded that even if the laws of Alberta were applicable to the
Colin Webster Trusts and the Protective Trust, I would still deny an order for
accounting.

[
116
]

Under
Alberta law, the question of whether an accounting is owed to an interested
person is summarized in
Waters' Law of Trusts
at pp. 1065 and 1066:

Persons with vested or contingent
interests are entitled to seek an inspection or request the court for an
accounting... As far as asking the court for an accounting is concerned, none
of these persons has an absolute right. As we have seen, harassing the trustee
is vexatious litigation, and
whether the court will order an accounting
depends entirely upon the court's discretion and the circumstances of the case
.
Only where the trustee can be shown to be in default of his duties will this
normally be given.

[emphasis added]

[
117
]

A
trustee potentially owes a duty to provide information to a large range of
beneficiaries including those with present interest in the trust property,
those with a contingent interest in remainder property, or those who are only
an object of a discretionary trust. See:
Re Ballard Estate
(1994),
1994 CanLII 7513 (ON CTGD)
, 20
O.R. (3d) 350 (Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)) at pp. 355-356 citing
Halsbury's Laws
of England
, 4th ed., vol. 48 (London: Butterworths, 1985) at para. 830. See
also
Halsbury's Laws of England
, 4th ed., vol. 48 (London: Butterworths,
2007) at para. 962.

[
118
]

The
Ontario Court of Appeal confirmed that the circumstances of the case are key to
a court's decision as to whether a trustee is obliged to give copies of
accounts to potential beneficiaries. In
Sandford v. Porter

(1889), 16
O.A.R. 565 (Ont. C.A.) at pp. 571-572
:

The duty of a trustee or other
accounting party is to have his accounts always ready, to afford all reasonable
facilities for inspection and examination, and to give full information
whenever required... Cases may be imagined where it would be reasonable to
require, and when it might be the duty of the trustee to furnish, statements of
account... But
every case depends on its own circumstances and must be
governed by reason and common sense
. Every one would see how unreasonable
and absurd it would be to say it was the duty of an executor of a large estate
which had been going on for a number of years, to furnish, on demand, to a
person interested, it might be in only a small share of the residue, a copy of
the estate accounts. In such a case the accounts might fill one or more large
ledgers, and other usual books of account. In such a case the legatee is
interested in, and entitled to see and examine, all the entries from first to
last. He may examine them and take copies or extracts and he is entitled to
reasonable explanation from the trustee of whatever requires explanation, but
he cannot require the trustee to make copies and extracts for him.

[emphasis added]

[
119
]

The
factors to consider when determining whether an accounting should be ordered
was recently discussed by the Privy Council in
Schmidt v. Rosewood Trust
Limited
at para. 67:

the recent cases also confirm (as
has been stated as long ago as
Re Cowin

(1886) 33 Ch D 179
) that no
beneficiary (and least of all a discretionary object) has any entitlement as of
right to disclosure of anything which can plausibly be described as a trust
document. Especially
when there are issues as to personal or commercial
confidentiality, the court may have to balance the competing interests of
different beneficiaries, the trustees themselves and third parties
.
Disclosure may have to be limited and safeguards may have to be put in place.
Evaluation of the claims of a beneficiary (and especially of a discretionary
object) may be an important part of the balancing exercise which the court has
to perform on the materials placed before it.
In many cases the court may
have no difficulty in concluding that an applicant with no more than a
theoretical possibility of benefit ought not to be granted any relief
.

[emphasis added]

[
120
]

With
respect to issues of confidentiality, the Ontario Court in
Re Ballard Estate

cautioned against allowing a trustee to rely on the doctrine of privilege to
deny access to information regarding the administration of a trust at p. 356:

It is untenable that in such
circumstances, a trustee can invoke the doctrine of privilege merely because
the residual legatee has received or will receive nothing under the trustee's
administration when the reason for that outcome may be the trustee's own
misconduct.

Moreover, the cases have stated
that, whatever approach to the claim of privilege is taken, in actions where
the beneficiary is alleging lack of good faith or breach of fiduciary duty,
this information is to be made available to him or her.

[
121
]

The
parties are in agreement that under Alberta law, it is a matter of the court's
discretion whether an accounting will be ordered.

[
122
]

For
the Colin Webster Trusts and the Protective Trust, Brenda Webster-Tweel has at
least a contingent interest in the funds within these trusts. Presumably she is
seeking the accountings for these two trusts to determine whether these funds
were prematurely depleted to her detriment. The response to these concerns,
however, is found within the trust deeds themselves.

[
123
]

The
Colin Webster Trusts specifically allows for the depletion of the capital
within the trusts through a provision allowing for encroachment upon the
capital of the trust property for the benefit of Lorne Webster; as such,
challenging the depletion of the Colin Webster Trust would be difficult. The
other property remaining in the Colin Webster Trusts have very minimal value;
approximately one dollar remains. Thus, I find that Brenda Webster-Tweel stands
to benefit little or nothing from the accountings from the Colin Webster Trust.

[
124
]

For
the Protective Trust, until the time of his death, Lorne Webster was able to
change the way in which the trust property would devolve by amending his 2000
Marriage Contract; it was possible for him to remove Brenda from the list of
potential beneficiaries pursuant to the 2000 Marriage Contract. Until Lorne
Webster's death, Brenda only had a theoretical possibility of benefit, since
she could have predeceased her father or he could have changed his 2000
Marriage Contract to remove her as a beneficiary of the subsequent trusts. I
note also that Brenda has already been provided information pertaining to the
funds within the Protective Trust at the time that the Webster-Tweel Trust was
created. It is not clear why Brenda requires any further information about this
Protective Trust.

[
125
]

The
interest of the trustees, Royal Trust and Hallward, as well as the other
beneficiaries under the Colin Webster Trusts and individuals benefiting from
trusts created from the funds of the Protective Trust must also be considered.
I accept that the other beneficiaries, particularly Lorne's widow, may have
confidentiality interests which are triggered by Brenda's request for
accounting. I am also persuaded that the trustees have an interest in not being
required to account to individuals who have minimal interest in the trusts in
their charge. In this regard, I note also that the Royal Trust has already
provided accounting documents to Lorne Webster, the primary beneficiary of
these trusts.

[
126
]

For
these reasons, I find that it would be unreasonable to order an accounting for
either the Colin Webster Trusts or the Protective Trust.

[
127
]

In
light of this determination, I find it unnecessary to consider whether the
principles in the
Limitations Act
, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12 should be
applied to limit the scope of the accounting required.

Conclusion

[
128
]

Brenda
Webster-Tweel is not entitled to an accounting for the Colin Webster Trusts or
the Protective Trust. Both trusts are governed by Quebec law and the Defendants
have met their burden of proving that under Quebec law no accounting would be
ordered.

Webster-Tweel Trust

[
129
]

The
parties are in agreement that, regardless of whether Quebec or Alberta law
applies, Brenda is entitled to an accounting for this trust.

[
130
]

The
Respondents' expert, Dr. Talpis, concluded that pursuant to Quebec law
"the Applicant, as a beneficiary of the trust created in her favour under
the Children's and Grandchildren's Trusts pursuant to the marriage contract, is
entitled to annual accounts from 2004 because she is an actual
beneficiary."

[
131
]

Applying
the principles set out in
Sandford
and
Smidt
, I am satisfied that
in this situation, since Brenda Webster-Tweel is the primary beneficiary of the
Webster-Tweel Trust, she would be entitled to an accounting of some sort.

[
132
]

However,
Brenda Webster-Tweel has already received detailed financial statements for
this trust since its inception in the form of 'Investment Statements' and
'Capital and Revenue Transaction Statements'. She asserts that these documents
are insufficient, but fails to specify what additional documents or information
she is seeking to obtain from the trustees.

Conclusion

[
133
]

Absent
a request for specific additional documents and in light of the financial
statements which have already been given to Brenda, I find it unreasonable to
order further accounting for the Webster-Tweel Trust. Royal Trust and Mr.
Hallward were not in default of their duties as trustees.

3.         whether
this Court should issue an order requiring Royal Trust to provide accounting
records for the last 15 years on the basis of a contractual agreement between
Royal Trust and Brenda Webster-Tweel

Choice of Law - Contracts

[
134
]

The
proper law of the contract governs most contractual issues and is determined by
express or implied intention of the parties, or, if no intention is expressed
or implied, by judicial determination of the system of law with which the
transaction has the closest and most real and substantial connection (see
Castel
and Walker
, vol. 2 at pp. 31-3 to 31-5).

[
135
]

The
factors to consider when attempting to infer the intention of the parties
include: any choice of location for arbitrations or courts expressly stated to
have jurisdiction over disputes, a connection with a preceding transaction, the
nature and location of the subject matter of the contract, the residence of the
parties, and the head office of a corporation party to the contract (see
Castel
and Walker
, vol. 2 at pp. 31-4 to 31-5).

[
136
]

When
there is no express or implied intention as to applicable law, the question
becomes which system of law has the closest and most real connection with the
transaction. All the circumstances must be considered and the court looks to
factors such as the place of contracting, the place of performance, the place
of residence or business of the parties, and the nature of the subject matter
of the contract (see
Castel and Walker
, vol. 2 at p. 31-6).

Analysis

[
137
]

In
this case, Royal Trust and Brenda Webster-Tweel did not expressly agree upon
which province's laws would govern the purported contract. I also find that the
parties likely did not turn their minds to the issue at all, and it would be
inappropriate to infer the intention of the parties in this situation. Thus,
the proper law governing the contract is determined based on the system of law
with which the purported contract is most closely connected.

[
138
]

The
relevant factors for the purported contract show that the purported contract is
most closely connected to the laws of Alberta. The purported agreement is for
Royal Trust's office in Alberta to provide Brenda Webster-Tweel with copies of
accounting documents which are located in Alberta. Although the subject matter
of the contract is accounting documents for trusts governed by the laws of
Quebec, I find that since the place of performance is Alberta and one of the
contracting parties has an office in Alberta, the laws of Alberta are the
proper law of the contract.

Validity of Contract

[
139
]

The
essential elements required to form a legally enforceable contract are that
there must be an agreement between the parties and the agreement must be
supported by consideration (see G.H.L. Fridman,
The Law of Contract in
Canada
, 5th ed. (Toronto: ThomsonCarswell, 2006) at pp. 13, 81-82). The
agreement is reached when an offer is made by one party and accepted by the
other party (see
Fridman
at p. 45). There must also be an expressed or
implied intention to create a contract (see
Fridman
at p. 27).

[
140
]

In
certain situations, forebearance to sue can be valuable consideration at common
law (see
Fridman
at p. 94 and 95). See for example
British Columbia
(Attorney General) v. Deeks Sand & Gravel Co.
,
1956 CanLII 55 (SCC)
, [1956] S.C.R. 336 where
the Supreme Court upheld a compromise agreement when the claims were founded
upon an honest difference of opinion as to the construction of certain leases.
The Court noted that the compromise agreement involved concessions on both
sides and held at pp. 345-346: "In these circumstances, as it cannot be
said, in my opinion, that the provincial claims were either frivolous or
vexatious or other than "real" within the meaning of the authorities,
the compromise was a binding one."

[
141
]

The
Applicant's position is that a contract was formed during the telephone
conversation on June 2, 2005 between Brenda Webster-Tweel and Garry Kaye of
Royal Trust. The terms of this purported contract are that Royal Trust was to
provide Brenda with 15 years worth of records and Brenda would refrain from
applying to court to obtain an accounting. The Respondent's position, however,
is that its offer to provide 15 years worth of records through its October 26,
2005 letter was never accepted by the Applicant.

[
142
]

I
am persuaded by the Respondent's view of the June 2, 2005 meeting and
subsequent correspondence between the parties. Although Royal Trust offered to
provide 15 years worth of records to the Applicant, rather than accept these
records as sufficient, the Applicant continued to ask for a full accounting for
the entire duration of all the trusts. Royal Trust revoked its offer to provide
these records by its February 9, 2006 letter to the Applicant. As such, there
is no agreement between the parties and no contract was formed.

[
143
]

I
also do not find, on the facts, that there was a forebearance to sue by the
Applicant. The Applicant's position has always been that unless all the
requested records were provided, a court application would be made to obtain
the records. This position did not change when the Applicant asked for
"some of the records" they requested to be forwarded in accordance
with Royal Trust's October 26, 2005 letter. The Applicant never indicated that
she would not pursue a court application if the 15 years worth of records were
forwarded. As such, unlike the situation in
Deeks Sand & Gravel
,
there was no concession on the part of the Applicant which might make the
agreement to provide records binding.

[
144
]

Thus,
I find there is no basis to order Royal Trust to provide 15 years worth of
records to the Applicant.

Decision

[
145
]

Brenda
Webster-Tweel is not entitled to an accounting for the Colin Webster Trusts or
for the Protective Trust. The entitlement to an accounting is governed by the
laws applicable to the administration of the trusts, which is the laws of
Quebec. As proven through expert evidence, pursuant to the laws of Quebec,
Brenda Webster-Tweel would not be entitled to an accounting for these trusts.

[
146
]

Brenda
Webster-Tweel is not entitled to a further accounting for the Webster-Tweel
Trust. She has already received quarterly statements from the inception of this
trust, and, absent a request for specific additional documents, it is
unreasonable to order any further accounting.

[
147
]

There
is no basis on which to order Royal Trust to provide accounting records for the
last 15 years. There was never an agreement between the parties to provide
these records and there was no consideration flowing from the Applicant to
support such an agreement.
